headline: Election Day: the official same-point comparison across five states implies a national vote of about D-1.0 (±1.2) against 2022 and about D+3.5 (±1.3) against 2024 (four states), while the polls say D+8.9 and the app's forecast D+6.9. In the final Nov 2 files Florida is R+2.4 by registration on 5.46 million ballots against R+6.0 at one day out in 2022, Nevada D+5.6 on 753,056 against D+1.4, Colorado D+5.8 on 1.86 million against D+2.9, Iowa's absentee pool D+9.4 against D+18.7 and Pennsylvania's mail D+39.6 against D+48.3. The finals elsewhere lean Democratic: Jon Ralston has Nevada's Democrats up about 42,500 ballots with a Clark County firewall of 67,500-68,000 on nearly 760,000 votes, North Carolina closed at 2,816,821 early ballots (Republicans 26% of them against 31% in 2022), Georgia at 2,810,170 (+13% on 2022) and Michigan at more than 2.3 million (31.2% of active voters); but Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by 287,000 and Texas's closing days, Pennsylvania's mail returns finished 5% behind 2022 and Arizona's ballots are R+11,958 on Go Right Strategies' count.

compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024. Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania are computed from the state files by the update job (Florida 5,464,802 ballots in the Nov 2 file against the state's 2024 figures at one day out; Nevada 753,056 in the Nov 2 file; Colorado 1,859,900 through Nov 2; Iowa 149,325 absentees in the Nov 2 report; Pennsylvania 1,062,313 mail ballots through Nov 2); Maine is Call the Map's reading of the state file (211,791 ballots through Oct 26). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, Florida most of all because 2024's Republicans had moved to in-person early voting; against 2022 the official comparison is narrower and mixed (Florida R+2.4 vs. R+6.0, Nevada D+5.6 vs. D+1.4, Colorado D+5.8 vs. D+2.9, Iowa D+9.4 vs. D+18.7, Pennsylvania D+39.6 vs. D+48.3), and North Carolina's comparison is computed from the State Board's files.

bullets.title: The official comparison with 2022 ends at five states and a national vote of about D-1.0, where it sat all week; against 2024 it reads about D+3.5 on four states.
bullets.html: By registration, Florida's final Nov 2 file counts 5,464,802 ballots at R+2.4 (mail 854,486 Democrats to 696,887 Republicans; in person 1,210,626 to 1,497,656), against R+6.0 at one day out in 2022; Nevada's 753,056 ballots are D+5.6 (mail D+51,102, in person R+8,693) against D+1.4 at the same point in 2022; Colorado's 1,859,900 returned ballots are D+5.8 against D+2.9; Iowa's 149,325 absentees are D+9.4 against D+18.7; and Pennsylvania's 1,062,313 returned mail ballots are D+39.6 against D+48.3. The app's calibrated slopes turn those into +3.1, +3.6, +2.4, -2.1 and -1.9 points of margin and a pooled implied national vote of about D-1.0 (±1.2), against polls at D+8.9 and the app's forecast at D+6.9. Against 2024 the same files read better for Democrats: Florida R+2.4 against R+10.2 (worth about +6.6), Nevada D+5.6 against R+3.8 (+8.0), Colorado D+5.8 against D+1.8 (+3.4) and Arizona's county compilation at R+0.7 on 1,648,197 ballots against R+8.4 (+6.5) pool to about D+3.5 (±1.3); Pennsylvania's mail at D+39.6 against D+22.6 is worth about +3.8 (±3.5) and Iowa's D+9.4 against R+1.1 about +2.3 (±3.3). Arizona has a 2024 baseline but none for 2022.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Nov 2
UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Nov 2)
Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Nov 2
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Nov 4, 2022 (the 2022 Florida baseline)

bullets.title: Nevada: Democrats finished early voting up about 42,500 ballots with a Clark County firewall of 67,500-68,000 on nearly 760,000 votes; Ralston says Lombardo probably needs about 55 percent of the remaining votes.
bullets.html: Jon Ralston's 8 p.m. Nov 2 entry: Democrats lead by about 42,500 ballots after the last mail batches, the Clark firewall is 67,500 (68,000 if the remaining mail is accepted overnight), nearly 760,000 votes are in and he expects a final of about 1.1 to 1.2 million; Clark's mail margin that day was about half that of recent batches; Lombardo 'probably needs about 55 percent of the remaining votes to have a chance' and Republicans need 'a very large, 2022-like share of the vote tomorrow.' His 7 a.m. Nov 2 entry: a 43,000-plus lead, just under 6 percent, Clark at 66,000 (13.7 percent), turnout 732,000 (739,000 with returned but unaccepted mail), 35 percent of actives; Clark's 498,914 ballots were 12.6% above the 442,930 at this point in 2022 though turnout as a share of actives was 33.0% against 33.6%; 2022's Election Day was R 101,090, D 53,368, other 59,804 on 215,517 ballots, and a 250,000-ballot Election Day at those ratios (R 117,500, D 62,500, other 70,000) would be a 55,000-ballot Republican edge, 'a best-case scenario for the GOP' that 'would make some races a bit closer but not change outcomes,' except perhaps the governor's race. The state's Nov 2 file reads D+5.6 on 753,056 ballots against D+1.4 at this point in 2022 and R+3.8 in 2024.
sources: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Nov 2)
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; county and Secretary of State data

bullets.title: North Carolina closed early voting at a record 2,816,821 ballots, 35.7% of registered voters, with Republicans 26% of them against 31% in 2022 and Black voters' ballots 1.5 times 2022's.
bullets.html: WBTV's reading of the NC FreeEnterprise Foundation tracker (Nov 1): 2,816,821 early ballots, 35.7% of registered voters against 29.0% turnout in 2022's early period; Democrats 38% ('steady'), unaffiliated 35% (30% in 2022), Republicans 26% (31% in 2022); turnout above 2022 in 97 of 100 counties; Black voters nearly 600,000 ballots, '1.5x' 2022; voters 18-25 more than 200,000, nearly double. Michael Bitzer (Nov 1): 2.8 million early ballots, about 36% of registered voters; mail accepted 92,395, about 3.3%; 46% of registered Democrats have voted, 32% ahead of their 2022 numbers, unaffiliated voters nearly 1 million, up 52%, Republicans up 9% on 2022; on his assumptions the early vote is about 55% Democratic to 38% Republican, Republicans would need about 58% of the remaining registrants for a tie, and the electorate looks 'more like 2018 than 2022.' Call the Map: D+12.2 against D+6.8 at the same point in 2022, ballots up 31%. The app's own file carries the official comparison (2,819,922 accepted ballots through Nov 1).
sources: Michael Bitzer, Center for NC Politics, Nov 1
bullets.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; Bitzer is a nonpartisan academic; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Georgia finished at 2,810,170 ballots, 13% above 2022's early vote, with Democratic-primary voters outnumbering Republican-primary voters 883,000 to 644,000 and the Black share up to 32.4%.
bullets.html: Secretary of State figures (Atlanta News First, Oct 30): 2,810,170 ballots, 2,691,841 in person and 118,329 absentee, 37.3% of registered voters; 2022's in-person midterm record was nearly 2.3 million and its overall early record about 2.5 million. The AJC (Oct 31): more than 2.8 million, up 13% on the 2022 midterm; mail and electronic ballots 4.2% of the early vote against nearly 9% in 2022; white voters 52.6% of ballots against 58.2% 'at this point in 2022,' Black voters 32.4% against 30.2% (and 26.8% at the same stage of 2024), Hispanic 3.7% against 2%; voters 18-29 11%, voters 50 and over nearly 65%; 883,000-plus Democratic-primary voters against about 644,000 Republican-primary voters; Harris-strong precincts cast about 60,000 more early ballots than Trump-strong precincts, where 2022's gap was about 1,000; more than 630,000 early voters skipped 2022 and more than 435,000 2022 Election Day voters voted early; about 1.9 million registered voters in Trump strongholds and 1.8 million in Harris strongholds had not voted.
sources: Atlanta Journal-Constitution (Greg Bluestein and Charles Minshew), Oct 31
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; Georgia has no party registration, so party is primary history

bullets.title: Texas: a record 7.7 million early votes, 40.5% of registered voters, against 5.5 million in 2022; Republican-primary voters finished ahead of Democratic-primary voters among in-person ballots, 2,238,247 to 2,100,396.
bullets.html: The Texas Tribune (Nov 1, preliminary): more than 7.7 million early votes, 40.5% turnout, past 2018's record; 2022's early vote was 5.5 million (31%) and 2024's 9 million (49%); registration above 19 million, up 2.2% on November 2024. The Secretary of State's count as of Friday Oct 30 was 7,410,631, 38.92% of 19,041,684 registered voters (CBS Texas). theoelections (as of Oct 30): 7,744,549 early ballots, 7,463,553 in person and 280,996 by mail; in-person ballots from Republican-primary-only voters 2,238,247 (30.0%) against Democratic-primary-only voters' 2,100,396 (28.1%), both 185,982 (2.5%), no primary 2,938,928 (39.4%); the mail runs 32.8% Democratic-only (92,275) to 26.2% Republican-only (73,688). At the same point in 2022 Republican-primary voters led by 400,000 on Derek Ryan's count (NBC 5, Oct 27). Mark Jones: 'We're not going to hit presidential levels, but this is definitely high turnout'; Democratic strategist Matt Angle: 'That doesn't mean Democrats are going to win.'
sources: Texas Tribune (Colleen Deguzman) via KSAT, Nov 1
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; theoelections is an independent tracker; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

bullets.title: Florida: R+2.4 in the final Nov 2 file, with Republicans up 287,000 in person and Democrats up 158,000 by mail; 49% of registered Democrats and about 38% of registered Republicans have voted.
bullets.html: The Division of Elections' Nov 2 file (the app's official comparison) has 3,467,810 in-person ballots, 1,497,656 Republican to 1,210,626 Democratic (R+287,030), and 1,996,992 mail ballots returned, 854,486 Democratic to 696,887 Republican (D+157,599): 40.2% Republican to 37.8% Democratic on 5,464,802 ballots, from R+2.5 on Nov 1, R+1.0 on Oct 27 and D+6.7 at twenty days out. WFLA (Nov 2): early voting closed with Republicans 1,497,472 in person to Democrats 1,210,445 and no-party voters 668,396, against a Republican in-person edge of 1,167,529 to 675,629 in 2022 and 'over 1 million votes' in 2024; mail as of 11:03 a.m. Monday was 832,634 Democratic to 678,784 Republican and keeps counting to 7 p.m. Tuesday. WLRN (Nov 2): 5.4 million of 13.7 million registered voters have voted, 69% of 2022's total turnout; 49% of registered Democrats against 38.2% of Republicans and 31% of the 3.3 million no-party voters, in a state where Republicans hold a 1.5 million registration edge and out-turned Democrats by about 600,000 in 2022. Nikki Fried: 'In every county in this state, Democrats are showing up at rates that we have not seen in years'; Byron Donalds: 'there are going to be a lot of voters showing up on election day.' At one day out in 2022 the state was R+6.0, and at the same point in 2024 R+10.2.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Nov 2
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Nov 4, 2022 (the 2022 Florida baseline)
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; Fried is the Florida Democratic chair and Donalds the Republican nominee for governor

bullets.title: Turnout without party: Michigan finished at more than 2.3 million (31.2% of active voters), Wisconsin's 777,739 absentees already exceed 2022's final, Pennsylvania's mail ended 5% behind 2022 and Arizona is R+11,958.
bullets.html: Michigan (Secretary of State, Nov 2): more than 2.3 million ballots, 31.2% of 7.42 million active registered voters; 743,450 early in-person votes over the nine days ending Nov 1 (114,420 on the final Sunday) and 1,569,715 absentee ballots returned as of 7 a.m. Nov 2 of 2,174,646 requested. Wisconsin (The Center Square via Yahoo, Nov 2, Elections Commission data): 777,739 absentee ballots received, above the 741,795 returned in all of 2022, with 463,491 cast in person against 318,130 in 2022; the comparison is to 2022's final, not its same point. Pennsylvania (Call the Map, state file through Nov 2): returns 5% below the same point in 2022, D+39.6 against D+48.7; the state's Nov 2 file has 1,062,313 returned of 1,297,749 requested (Democrats 687,732, Republicans 267,388). Arizona (Go Right Strategies' county compilation, Nov 2, 12:04 p.m. ET): 1,648,197 ballots, Republicans 625,143 (37.9%), Democrats 613,185 (37.2%), other 409,869, R+11,958; Maricopa 973,135 at R+5,029, Pima 280,001 at D+55,043; the lead was R+12,335 a day earlier. Colorado: 1,859,900 ballots through Nov 2 at D+5.8 (the app's panel). Maine: Call the Map has absentee returns 39% above 2022's same point.
sources: The Center Square (Jon Styf) via Yahoo, Nov 2
Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Nov 2
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets and an independent tracker; Go Right Strategies is a Republican consulting firm

bullets.title: Nationally, 58.7 million have voted, past 2022's 45.9 million; Call the Map's seven day-by-day states are up 17% on 2022, and the registered-party gap moved toward Republicans in four of them.
bullets.html: UF Election Lab counted 58,677,062 ballots across 49 reporting jurisdictions in the app's Nov 3 file (26,779,541 by mail, 31,897,521 in person), against 45,920,446 early votes in all of 2022; CBS News (Nov 2) put the lab's count at more than 57 million, about 32 million in person and 25 million by mail, with New York past 1.7 million early votes and California past 6 million returned mail ballots. Call the Map (Nov 2, 5:28 p.m. ET): 54,251,912 ballots in 47 states; its seven states comparable day by day with 2022 are up 17% together (North Carolina +31%, Maine +39%, Iowa +36%, Colorado +19%, Florida +13%, Nevada's Clark mail +14%, Pennsylvania -5%), and the registered-party gap moved toward Republicans in four of the seven (Pennsylvania D+48.7 to D+39.6, Iowa D+18.7 to D+12.3, Nevada's Clark mail D+23.5 to D+20.6, Maine D+25.5 to D+24.1) and toward Democrats in North Carolina (D+6.9 to D+12.2), Colorado (D+3.2 to D+6.7) and Florida (R+6.7 to R+2.5). G. Elliott Morris (Nov 2): new voters cast 8.3% of North Carolina's early ballots against 7.4% at the same point in 2022 and are 'younger' and 'more Latino' than 2022's; he expects a Democratic turnout edge 'at least as big as 2018's in most states.' Newsweek (Oct 31, UF Election Lab): in the party-registration states, Democrats 43% and Republicans 32% of ballots.
bullets.aff: McDonald's lab is nonpartisan; Call the Map is an independent tracker; Morris is an independent analyst who works with L2 data

calendar_note: Election Day. Early in-person voting has ended everywhere; Pennsylvania's mail ballots must reach county offices by 8 p.m. and Florida's by 7 p.m. Polls close from 6 p.m. ET (Indiana, Kentucky) through 7 p.m. (Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia, most of Florida), 7:30 (North Carolina, Ohio), 8 p.m. (Maine, Pennsylvania, most of Michigan, Texas), 9 p.m. (Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Arizona), 10 p.m. (Nevada) and after midnight (Alaska).
cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 49 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 29-Nov 2) when these comparisons were compiled on Election Day morning; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison with 2022 (Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania) ends where it spent the final week, implying a national vote of about D-1.0 (±1.2): in the final Nov 2 files Florida is R+2.4 by registration against R+6.0 at one day out in 2022, Nevada D+5.6 against D+1.4, Colorado D+5.8 against D+2.9, Iowa's absentee pool D+9.4 against D+18.7 and Pennsylvania's mail D+39.6 against D+48.3; against 2024, Florida (R+2.4 vs. R+10.2), Nevada (D+5.6 vs. R+3.8), Colorado (D+5.8 vs. D+1.8) and Arizona (R+0.7 vs. R+8.4) pool to about D+3.5 (±1.3), so the early vote fits a Democratic year without confirming polls at D+8.9 or the app's forecast at D+6.9. The final tallies in the states without party registration lean Democratic: Ralston has Nevada's Democrats up about 42,500 ballots with a Clark firewall of 67,500-68,000 on nearly 760,000 votes, North Carolina closed at 2,816,821 ballots with Republicans 26% of them against 31% in 2022, Georgia's 2,810,170 ballots include 883,000 Democratic-primary voters to 644,000 Republican-primary voters, and Michigan passed 2.3 million; but Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by 287,000 and Texas's closing days, Pennsylvania's mail finished 5% behind 2022 with Democratic returns down 12%, Call the Map's registered-party gap moved toward Republicans in four of its seven day-by-day states, and Arizona is R+11,958. The test is now Election Day itself: Ralston says Lombardo probably needs about 55 percent of the remaining Nevada votes and Republicans a 2022-like Election Day share, Bitzer says Republicans would need about 58% of North Carolina's remaining registrants, and about 235,000 of Pennsylvania's approved mail ballots were still outstanding.

signals.title: Nevada's Democrats finished early voting up about 42,500 ballots, with a Clark County firewall of 67,500-68,000 on nearly 760,000 votes and Washoe County D+5
signals.value: Jon Ralston, 8 p.m. Nov 2: Democrats lead by about 42,500 ballots after the final mail batches; Clark's firewall is 67,500 (68,000 if the remaining mail is accepted); nearly 760,000 votes are in, with a final of about 1.1 to 1.2 million expected. 7 a.m. Nov 2: a 43,000-plus lead, just under 6 percent; Clark 66,000 (13.7 percent); turnout 732,000, 35 percent of actives; Clark's 498,914 ballots are 12.6% above 2022's same point. Nov 1: Washoe, R+3 in registration, is D+5 in ballots; rurals R+30,000; mail 58 percent of the total.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. Ralston's 2022-ratio Election Day scenario (250,000 ballots, R 117,500, D 62,500) is a 55,000-ballot Republican edge that 'would make some races a bit closer but not change outcomes,' except perhaps the governor's race, where Lombardo 'probably needs about 55 percent of the remaining votes'; Clark's mail margin on the last day was about half the recent batches'. The state's Nov 2 file reads D+5.6 on 753,056 ballots against D+1.4 at this point in 2022 and R+3.8 in 2024 (the app's official panel).
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet (Jon Ralston); county and Secretary of State data

signals.title: North Carolina's final early vote is 2,816,821 ballots, 35.7% of registered voters, with Republicans 26% of them against 31% in 2022, Democrats 38% and Black voters' ballots 1.5 times 2022's
signals.value: WBTV (Nov 1, NC FreeEnterprise Foundation tracker): 2,816,821 early ballots, 35.7% of registered voters against 29.0% in 2022; Democrats 38%, unaffiliated 35% (30% in 2022), Republicans 26% (31%); turnout above 2022 in 97 of 100 counties; Black voters nearly 600,000, '1.5x' 2022; 18-25 more than 200,000, nearly double. Bitzer (Nov 1): 46% of registered Democrats have voted, 32% ahead of 2022; unaffiliated nearly 1 million, up 52%; Republicans up 9%; mail 92,395 (3.3%). Call the Map: D+12.2 against D+6.8 at the same point in 2022, ballots up 31%.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice; much of the surge is 2022 Election Day voters moving earlier, and Republicans outvoted Democrats on Election Day 2022. Bitzer's 55-38 modeled split rests on his assumptions (D 95/5, R 90/10, UNA 50/39), and he expects about 1.5 million more votes. The app's own file carries the official comparison.
signals.src: WBTV, Nov 1; Center for NC Politics (Michael Bitzer), Nov 1; Call the Map, Nov 1
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; Bitzer is a nonpartisan academic; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Georgia's 2,810,170 early ballots are 13% above 2022's, with Democratic-primary voters ahead of Republican-primary voters 883,000 to 644,000 and the Black share 32.4% against 30.2% at this point in 2022
signals.value: Secretary of State figures (Atlanta News First, Oct 30): 2,810,170 ballots, 2,691,841 in person and 118,329 absentee, 37.3% of registered voters; 2022's overall early record was about 2.5 million. AJC (Oct 31): up 13% on 2022; white voters 52.6% against 58.2% 'at this point in 2022,' Black 32.4% against 30.2% (26.8% at the same stage of 2024), Hispanic 3.7% against 2%; 883,000-plus Democratic-primary voters to about 644,000 Republican-primary voters; Harris-strong precincts cast about 60,000 more ballots than Trump-strong precincts, against a gap of about 1,000 in 2022; more than 630,000 early voters skipped 2022.
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration: primary history covers only some voters and the precinct comparison is to 2024's presidential vote. The electorate is old (voters 50 and over nearly 65%), mail is down to 4.2% of the early vote, and about 1.9 million registered voters in Trump strongholds had not voted against 1.8 million in Harris strongholds.
signals.src: Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Oct 31; Atlanta News First, Oct 30

signals.title: Texas's record 7.7 million early votes (40.5% of registered voters) are 2.2 million above 2022's, and Democratic-primary voters are far closer to Republican-primary voters than 2022's 400,000 Republican lead
signals.value: Texas Tribune (Nov 1, preliminary): more than 7.7 million early votes, 40.5% turnout, past 2018's record; 2022's early vote was 5.5 million (31%), 2024's 9 million (49%). Secretary of State count as of Oct 30: 7,410,631, 38.92% of 19,041,684 registered (CBS Texas). theoelections (Oct 30): 7,744,549 ballots, 7,463,553 in person and 280,996 by mail; Democratic-primary-only voters 2,100,396 (28.1%) of in-person ballots, Republican-primary-only 2,238,247 (30.0%), no primary 2,938,928 (39.4%); mail 32.8% Democratic-only to 26.2% Republican-only. At the same point in 2022 Republican-primary voters led by 400,000 (Derek Ryan via NBC 5, Oct 27).
signals.catch: No party registration: 'party' is primary history, 39% of in-person voters have none, and 2022's electorate was unusually Republican. Republican-primary voters won the closing days and finished ahead in person (the separate signal). Mark Jones: 'definitely high turnout'; Matt Angle (Democratic strategist): 'That doesn't mean Democrats are going to win.'
signals.src: Texas Tribune via KSAT, Nov 1; CBS Texas, Oct 31; theoelections, Oct 30; NBC 5 DFW, Oct 27
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlets and official data; theoelections is an independent tracker; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

signals.title: Texas's Republican close: Republican-primary voters finished ahead of Democratic-primary voters among in-person ballots, 2,238,247 to 2,100,396, after trailing through the first week
signals.value: theoelections (as of Oct 30, the final day): in-person ballots from Republican-primary-only voters 2,238,247 (30.0%) against Democratic-primary-only 2,100,396 (28.1%), both 185,982 (2.5%), no primary 2,938,928 (39.4%), on 7,463,553 in-person ballots; the Oct 28 count had Republicans ahead 1,757,395 to 1,699,975 and the Oct 29 count 1,905,771 to 1,824,245. Mail: 92,275 Democratic-only (32.8%) to 73,688 Republican-only (26.2%). Ryan's statewide Democratic-primary edge had fallen from about 115,000 after the first week to nearly 57,000 through Oct 28 (NBC 5; CBS Texas).
signals.catch: Primary history is not vote choice, and 39% of in-person voters have none. Against 2022, when Republican-primary voters led by 400,000 at this point, the electorate is still far more Democratic; the signal is the direction of the final days.
signals.src: theoelections, Oct 30; CBS Texas, Oct 29; NBC 5 DFW, Oct 27
signals.aff: theoelections is an independent tracker whose affiliation is not stated; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

signals.title: Florida's early vote ended R+2.4 in the final Nov 2 file, with Republicans up 287,000 in person and the lead growing every day of the final week
signals.value: Division of Elections file for Nov 2 (the app's official panel): 3,467,810 in-person ballots, 1,497,656 Republican to 1,210,626 Democratic (R+287,030); 1,996,992 mail ballots returned, 854,486 Democratic to 696,887 Republican (D+157,599); combined 40.2% Republican to 37.8% Democratic on 5,464,802 ballots, from R+2.5 on Nov 1, R+1.0 on Oct 27 and D+6.7 at twenty days out. WFLA (Nov 2): in-person early voting closed at Republicans 1,497,472, Democrats 1,210,445, no-party 668,396; mail as of 11:03 a.m. Monday 832,634 Democratic to 678,784 Republican. WLRN: 49% of registered Democrats have voted against 38.2% of Republicans.
signals.catch: The same-point comparison still favors Democrats: R+6.0 at one day out in 2022 and R+10.2 in 2024 (the app's official panel), and 2022's final early vote was R+6.4; Republicans' in-person edge was 491,900 in 2022 and over 1 million in 2024 (WFLA). Mail keeps arriving until 7 p.m. Tuesday and leans Democratic. Registration is not vote choice, and Republicans hold a 1.5 million registration edge.
signals.src: Florida Division of Elections daily file via the app's official comparison, Nov 2; WFLA via Yahoo, Nov 2; WLRN, Nov 2
signals.aff: Official data; WFLA and WLRN are nonpartisan outlets

signals.title: Pennsylvania's mail returns finished 5% behind 2022's same point at D+39.6 against D+48.7, with Democrats' returns down 12% and Republicans' up 14%
signals.value: Call the Map (state file through Nov 2): returns 5% below the same point in 2022; D+39.6 against D+48.7 at the same point in 2022, a 9.1-point move toward Republicans, the largest of its seven day-by-day states. Its Nov 1 reading of the Oct 31 file: Democrats 681,934 (down 12% from 771,898), Republicans 265,272 (up 14% from 233,284), unaffiliated and other 105,962 (up 4%). The state's Nov 2 file (the app's official panel): 1,062,313 returned of 1,297,749 requested, Democrats 687,732 (64.7%), Republicans 267,388 (25.2%), other 107,193; D+39.6 against D+48.3 in 2022 and D+22.6 in 2024.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year (D+48.3 at this point in 2022, when Republicans won the national vote), and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting; the state has no in-person early voting, so there is no in-person count to offset it. Call the Map notes 2022's file counted every ballot with a return date. The official comparison is on the app's panel, so this signal is the turnout picture only. About 235,000 approved ballots were still outstanding and must arrive by 8 p.m.
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file

signals.title: Arizona's early ballots are R+11,958 (0.7 points) by registration on 1.65 million through Nov 2, with Maricopa R+5,029 and Pima D+55,043
signals.value: Go Right Strategies' county compilation (Nov 2, 12:04 p.m. ET): 1,648,197 ballots returned, Republicans 625,143 (37.9%), Democrats 613,185 (37.2%), other 409,869 (24.9%), R+11,958; Maricopa (updated Nov 2, 11:36 a.m. ET) 973,135 at R+5,029; Pima 280,001 at D+55,043; the lead was R+12,335 on Nov 1 and R+13,526 on Oct 29, narrowing by 377 on 45,490 new ballots. The app's panel reads R+0.7 on 1,648,197 ballots in the Nov 2 file against R+8.4 at the same point in 2024 (worth about +6.5 points on its calibrated slope).
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice: Republicans have a registration edge near 300,000, so a lead this small means Democrats are returning ballots at a higher rate; there is no official statewide daily file, the compilation is from county reports on different schedules, and the app has no 2022 same-point baseline. Late-arriving early ballots dropped off on Election Day take days to count. The tracker is a Republican consulting firm.
signals.aff: Go Right Strategies is a Republican consulting firm; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Wisconsin's 777,739 absentee ballots already exceed 2022's final 741,795, with in-person absentees at 463,491 against 318,130 in 2022 while mail returns fell, most sharply in Democratic Milwaukee and Dane
signals.value: The Center Square (Nov 2, Elections Commission data): 777,739 absentee ballots received, above the 741,795 returned in all of 2022; 463,491 cast in person against 318,130 in 2022, leaving roughly 314,000 by mail; Milwaukee had received 48,311 absentee ballots as of 7 p.m. Friday. WPR (Oct 31, data as of Oct 30): 693,334 returned, about 50,000 more than 2022's same point; mail about 300,000 against about 384,000 in 2022 (down more than 20%), in-person about 394,000 against about 259,000 (up more than 50%); Milwaukee's mail down more than 25% and in-person up 45%, Dane's mail down more than 30% and in-person up about 50%, Washington's in-person up about 75%, Waukesha's up more than 40%.
signals.catch: No party registration, so this is turnout only, both parties pushed voters away from mail, and The Center Square's comparison is to 2022's final rather than its same point. The Democratic counties' totals closed the gap as in-person voting ran through Nov 1. Handrick: 'While the early returns are encouraging for the GOP, they are not predictive.'
signals.src: The Center Square (Jon Styf) via Yahoo, Nov 2; WPR via Urban Milwaukee, Oct 31; Dairyland Sentinel (Joe Handrick), Oct 27
signals.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; The Center Square is a conservative-leaning nonprofit newsroom; the Dairyland Sentinel analysis is on a conservative-leaning site by a former Republican legislator

signals.title: Michigan finished at more than 2.3 million ballots, 31.2% of active voters, with 743,450 early in-person votes that did not exist in 2022 and 1.57 million absentees returned
signals.value: Secretary of State (Nov 2): more than 2.3 million ballots cast, a 31.2% turnout rate of 7.42 million active registered voters; 743,450 early in-person votes through the close of the nine-day period on Nov 1, 114,420 of them on the final Sunday; 1,569,715 absentee ballots returned as of 7 a.m. Nov 2 of 2,174,646 requested (2,023,195 on the permanent mail list). The department's Oct 27 release had 1,176,375 absentees returned against 1,126,246 a week before Election Day 2022; Detroit's clerk projects 40-45% turnout against 34% in 2022 (CBS Detroit).
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction, and the department cautions that higher early numbers 'do not necessarily mean' higher overall turnout; the release gives no 2022 same-point total for all early ballots. A Democratic congresswoman's Nov 1 endorsement of the Republican Senate nominee is the race's late variable.
signals.src: Michigan Secretary of State, Nov 2; CBS News Detroit, Oct 30

signals.title: Maine's absentee returns are 36% ahead of 2022 at the same point (275,563 against about 202,000), and Democrats are about half of them
signals.value: Secretary of State figures as of Thursday Oct 29 (WGME): 313,611 absentee ballots requested, 312,874 issued, 275,563 returned and accepted, 'more than 276,000' against 'more than 202,000' at this point in 2022; a return rate above 88% against almost 81%; more than 152,000 cast in the presence of a clerk; Secretary Bellows: 'We are seeing the requests and the returns way up over the last midterm election in 2022.' Press Herald (Oct 28, data through Oct 27): nearly 222,000 accepted, 32% above 2022's same point and 20% below 2024's; about half of voters so far are Democrats (36% of registered Democrats have voted), Republicans about 22% of returns (18% of registered Republicans), unaffiliated more than a quarter; in the 2nd District Republicans are 27% of early votes against 33% at this point in 2024.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice, and against 2022 the party gap is about a point narrower (Call the Map's Oct 26 reading: D+27.8 against D+28.7), so the Democratic reading comes from turnout and the 2024 comparison; unaffiliated voters decide the Collins race. In-person absentee voting ended Oct 29.
signals.src: WGME (Allyson LaPierre), Oct 29; Portland Press Herald (Ethan Horton), Oct 28

signals.title: Nevada's statewide in-person vote finished Republican (R+8,693 in the final Nov 2 file), and mail is 59% of the total
signals.value: The state's Nov 2 file (the app's official panel): in-person ballots statewide 121,645 Republican to 112,952 Democratic (R+8,693) on 308,025, mail 183,151 Democratic to 132,049 Republican (D+51,102) on 445,031. Ralston (Nov 2): Clark's mail margin on the final day was about half that of recent batches; Nov 1: mail is 58 percent of the statewide total, Clark's mail margin 'close to 2-to-1,' rurals R+30,000.
signals.catch: Democrats are shifting from mail to in person, which the county-wide figures absorb (Clark overall is 67,500-68,000 against about 24,000 at this point in 2022); the in-person lead is small on 308,000 ballots. Registration is not vote choice.
signals.src: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Nov 2); Nevada Independent, Nov 2
signals.aff: Secretary of State data; Ralston is a nonpartisan journalist

signals.title: Call the Map: the registered-party gap moved toward Republicans in four of the seven states comparable day by day with 2022, led by Pennsylvania (9.1 points) and Iowa (6.4)
signals.value: Call the Map (Nov 2, 5:28 p.m. ET): 54,251,912 ballots in 47 states; the seven day-by-day states are up 17% on 2022 together, six of seven ahead of pace; 'the registered party gap moved toward Republicans' in Pennsylvania (D+48.7 to D+39.6), Iowa (D+18.7 to D+12.3), Nevada's Clark mail (D+23.5 to D+20.6) and Maine (D+25.5 to D+24.1), and toward Democrats in North Carolina (D+6.9 to D+12.2), Colorado (D+3.2 to D+6.7) and Florida (R+6.7 to R+2.5); Oklahoma, on fewer days, R+8.5 against R+14.9. Newsweek (Oct 31, UF Election Lab): in the party-registration states, Democrats 43%, Republicans 32%, others 25%.
signals.catch: Three of the four Republican moves are in mail-only or mail-heavy counts (Pennsylvania, Iowa's absentees, Clark mail) where Democrats are shifting to in person, and Maine's is 1.4 points; the app's official panel, which weights by mode, turns the same five-state picture into about D-1.0 nationally. Democrats' 2022 early-vote edge preceded a national vote they lost by about 3 points, which is why the edge alone says little.
signals.src: Call the Map, Nov 2; Newsweek (Hugh Cameron), Oct 31
signals.aff: Call the Map is an independent tracker; UF Election Lab is nonpartisan

signals.title: A record 58.7 million have voted, past 2022's 45.9 million, with turnout gains concentrated among Black, Hispanic and young voters and voters who skipped 2022
signals.value: UF Election Lab: 58,677,062 ballots in the app's Nov 3 file (49 jurisdictions; 26.8 million by mail, 31.9 million in person) against 45,920,446 in all of 2022; CBS News (Nov 2) put the count at more than 57 million. Newsweek (Oct 31): Democrats 43% and Republicans 32% of ballots in party-registration states; the AP found Texas's early vote up 50% on 2022 and South Carolina's up 83%. Georgia's Black share is 32.4% against 30.2% at this point in 2022 (AJC); North Carolina's Black voters cast 1.5 times 2022's ballots and voters 18-25 nearly doubled (WBTV); G. Elliott Morris (Nov 2): new voters cast 8.3% of North Carolina's early ballots against 7.4% at the same point in 2022, are 'younger' and 'more Latino,' and he expects a Democratic turnout edge 'at least as big as 2018's in most states.'
signals.catch: Turnout is not vote choice, and Election Day was Republican in 2022; the national party split covers only the registration states, and Morris's party readings are L2's modeled split. DDHQ's Skelley: 'we must be careful not to divine with certainty winners and losers from the entrails of AB/EV data.'
signals.src: UF Election Lab, Nov 3; CBS News, Nov 2; Newsweek, Oct 31; AJC, Oct 31; WBTV, Nov 1; G. Elliott Morris, Nov 2
signals.aff: UF Election Lab is nonpartisan; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor; Morris is an independent analyst
